task.decision_user: Airport operations officer or airport wildlife hazard biologist receiving the strike report, deciding whether to escalate immediately (maintenance inspection, engine borescope, operator notification) and whether to re-prioritise that species/season in the airport's wildlife hazard management plan.

task.outcome_horizon: Same event: severity is established by inspection after the aircraft returns to service and is coded by the NWSD manager, usually within days; records are subsequently revised (LUPDATE), so this is a coded outcome, not a scheduled future event.
task.population: Reported civil-aircraft wildlife strikes with incident_date from 1990-01-01 through 2022-12-31, state in the 50 U.S. states or DC, at least one of ac_class or ac_mass present, and a DAMAGE value in N, M, M?, S or D. Eligibility is otherwise strike-time: date, location, aircraft descriptors and reported encounter facts. The one later quantity used in eligibility is the damage code itself, and only to drop unlabelled rows.
task.prediction_time: At the strike report, on the day of the strike, before the post-flight maintenance inspection and before laboratory species identification. Features are aircraft descriptors, encounter geometry, pilot observations, date/location and operator class; DAMAGE and all post-strike fields are excluded.
task.question: Given only what is known when a wildlife strike is reported, will the aircraft be assessed as substantially damaged or destroyed (ICAO major damage)?
task.simple_references: Majority class (about 2 percent positive in the frozen labelled 1990-2022 population, because unlabelled rows are dropped; the FAA's published 1 percent covers all reports); a train-only calendar-and-identity control using only month, state and ac_mass; an aircraft-mass-only control. No persistence baseline applies because the unit is one independent strike event, not a panel, so there is no prior state to carry forward.
task.split_policy: Fixed cut on INCIDENT_DATE, no random resampling: train 1990-01-01 to 2013-12-31; eval 2014-01-01 to 2018-12-31; holdout 2019-01-01 to 2022-12-31. No embargo is required inside the series because each row is one independent strike and every feature is fixed at strike time, so a later row cannot reveal an earlier label; the 2022-12-31 end cut is a reporting/validation lag buffer of about 3.7 years against a snapshot current to August 2026. Boundaries are frozen before any modelling.
task.target: 1 if DAMAGE is S (substantial) or D (destroyed); 0 if DAMAGE is N (none), M (minor) or M? (undetermined level). Rows with a blank DAMAGE are dropped, not labelled 0.
task.usefulness: Substantial damage is not a field the reporter predicts: it is an adjudicated ICAO severity category that must be inferred from aircraft configuration, encounter geometry and coarse animal-size cues, and identical circumstances mean very different things for a two-seat trainer and a twin-jet airliner. The task is to build an intake-triage score and to test whether that relationship survives 30 years of fleet-mix change, reporting-practice change and a tenfold rise in report volume; the temporal drift, not the label, is the hard part.

cross_row_audit.auxiliary_files_review: Only the three declared CSVs are produced; no auxiliary evaluation files.
cross_row_audit.rationale: Each row is an independent strike event. No cross-row joins, aggregate rates or label-derived features are shipped.

limitations: Current-vintage FAA export; no full-row availability ledger. Historical availability of strike-report fields is assumed, so training label timing is unverified.
Voluntary reporting is biased toward damaging strikes, so the positive rate is not an aircraft-level risk estimate.
DAMAGE is an adjudicated code selected after the event; it is used only as the target and is not a feature.

Blank DAMAGE rows are dropped, which is an outcome-availability filter and not a random sample; the prior build measured a realized positive rate near 2.3 percent (3,311 of 142,871) in the frozen population, above the FAA's published 1 percent, because unlabelled rows are removed before the rate is formed.

NUM_STRUCK and NUM_SEEN are ordinal bands on the report form, so the animal-number features carry band membership rather than an exact count; a strike with 3 animals and one with 10 animals share a single category, and a raw integer entered in the workbook is folded into the band containing it.
SPECIES and other post-strike or part-inspection fields are excluded even though species mass is a strong damage predictor.

The selected member in this snapshot is Public.xlsx sheet Sheet1; the builder still resolves roles by normalised alias and fails with the selected member, the observed header list and the unresolved role names if the publisher renames a field.

Rows with OPID tokens that are not three-letter airline codes and not BUS, PVT, GOV or MIL are counted, left missing and never guessed into a class, so operator information is lost for that share; no emitted value falls outside the documented vocabulary.
No persistence reference applies because each row is an independent strike event; the calendar/identity reference uses state, month and ac_mass and must be fit on training labels only.
No label-derived group-rate features are shipped; any reference rate must use only training labels whose outcome windows closed before each scored row.

selection.evidence: Eligibility uses incident_date, state, ac_class, ac_mass and nonblank DAMAGE; DAMAGE is the adjudicated target and is not a feature. Blank DAMAGE is dropped, not labelled 0.

vintage.evidence: FAA Wildlife Strike Database current export; records are edited and consolidated after reporting, and the download is a current snapshot rather than a historical register.

limitations: Strike reporting is voluntary and FAA states an overall bias toward reporting damaging strikes, so the 1.2% positive rate is a reporting artefact and not an aircraft-level risk of damage.

SPECIES is excluded even though the FAA's own analysis finds body mass the best single predictor of damage, because identification is usually done after the strike (Smithsonian Feather Lab, 24 hours to 10 days); SIZE is a coarse pilot-perceived proxy, so the frozen feature set is deliberately weaker than published species-based models.

The label is an adjudicated code selected by the NWSD manager from the report and can be revised; the snapshot is current-vintage, so this shows what can be reconstructed retrospectively, not that the damage code was available to an operator at the time.
Dropping rows with blank DAMAGE is a label-availability filter applied after the event and may correlate with reporting quality, so the modelling population is not a random sample of strikes.

17 U.S.C. Sec. 105 is a U.S. domestic basis only; no worldwide dedication is asserted and some jurisdictions may still protect the compilation, so non-U.S. re-users must check local law. Nothing here overrides any third-party right.

Strike reports are third-party submissions; to avoid personal data and third-party text the release drops REPORTED_NAME, REPORTED_TITLE, REG, FLT, REMARKS and COMMENTS, and uses only coded and numeric fields.

Fleet mix and reporting practice drift heavily across 1990-2022 (reports rise roughly tenfold and the damaging share falls from 18% to about 4%), so the chronological holdout tests transport under drift rather than stationarity.
Positives are rare enough that the 2019-2022 holdout should be expected to contain only several hundred positive events, so subgroup and calibration estimates there will be noisy.
